newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan sets up panel for land-backed problem loans.
newsitem.headline: Japan sets up panel for land-backed problem loans.

text.p: Japan set up a panel on Tuesday to tackle the tough issue of collecting problem loans in the form of land collateral, a Ministry of Finance (MOF) official said.

The panel, joined by officials from the ministries of finance, construction and justice and the National Land Agency, will discuss how to increase liquidity in the property market to facilitate collection of problem loans, the official said.
"It is important to increase the liquidity of collateralised land... However, the environment is tough as land prices are continuing to fall," the official told reporters.a
"It would be difficult to reach a conclusion unless all parties involved discuss the issue," the official said.

The panel, also joined by officials from the Deposit Insurance Corp of Japan (DIC), the Housing Loan Administration Corp (HLAC), the Resolution and Collection Bank (RCB), and officials from the Tokyo and Osaka prefectural governments, plans to make an interim report by the middle of next year, she said.
The majority of real estate put up as collateral for problem loans is located in Tokyo and Osaka, she said.

DIC is a semi-governmental body set up to protect depositors from bank failures. HLAC inherited assets from failed mortgage firms, known as "jusen", while the RCB aims to bail out collapsed credit unions.
Analysts have said that if HLAC starts selling the property put up as collateral for loans at the failed mortgage firms, land prices are likely to fall further due to slack demand.

The panel will look into the securitisation or liquidation of unrecoverable loans backed by land collateral, stimulation of the real estate market, and public utilisation of assets put up as collateral in big cities like Tokyo and Osaka.
Officials from the banking, securities and real estate industries will attend panel sessions to make concrete proposals to increase liquidity in collateral land.

The Resolution Trust Corp of the United States successfully recovered debts following the savings and loan crisis of the 1980s, but the conditions of the real estate market in Japan are different from those in the United States, making it hard for Japan to follow the U.S. example, the MOF official said.

Separately, an advisory council to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has been reviewing the nation's basic policy concerning land, she said, adding that the council is expected to make a final proposal by December.
